### Tests keeps each commit's run (2026-11-08)

abscls-ckqj. The workflow Tests had the concurrency group `tests-<ref>` with `cancel-in-progress` (since 2026-10-15,
with no reason recorded beyond a sentence in its header). A push to `dev` then cancelled the run of the commit before
it. A release takes only a commit whose run passed (docs/hosting.md, "Deploy, check and roll back"), so a cancelled
commit could not be released on its own result. The pre-push hook of abscls-fa50 refused such pushes, to protect the
result.

- **Decided:** the group is `tests-<sha>`, with no cancel. Each commit keeps its run, and no push waits. GitHub's
  rules ([workflow syntax, `concurrency`](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#concurrency)):
  a group runs one run at a time, and by default it keeps one pending run. A new pending run cancels the one that
  waits. So `cancel-in-progress: false` on `tests-<ref>` is not enough: a third push would cancel the middle commit's
  run. `queue: max` on `tests-<ref>` keeps up to 100 pending runs, but it runs them one at a time: with a Linux job of
  up to 40 minutes, each push would wait for the results of the pushes before it.
- **A re-run or a manual run of one commit** takes that commit's group. A re-run keeps its run's commit
  ([re-running workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-workflow-runs/re-run-workflows-and-jobs)),
  and a manual run (`workflow_dispatch`) takes the last commit of its branch
  ([events](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#workflow_dispatch)).
  While a run of that commit is in progress, the new run waits and cancels nothing. A second run that comes while one
  waits cancels the one that waits. A manual run on `main` after a release takes the same group as `dev`'s run of
  that commit.
- **Deploy is unchanged.** Its group stays `deploy-<ref>` with no cancel (`deploy.yml`). Deploys run one at a time,
  and an older commit never deploys after a newer one. A deploy that waits is cancelled by a newer push's deploy, as
  before. Only the Tests workflow changed.
- **The cost:** runs for older commits use runner time, and they count toward the limit of concurrent jobs (two jobs
  for each run). A fast series of pushes can queue the jobs of later runs behind the earlier ones. The repository is
  public, so the standard runners cost no minutes.
- **The hook** (`.githooks/pre-push`) no longer refuses. It could not guard each commit's result: it worked only in a
  clone with `core.hooksPath` set, it did not see a push from the web interface or with `--no-verify`, and two pushes
  in the seconds before GitHub made a run both passed. It now names each run still going on `dev` with the
  `scripts/ci-watch` line, and lets the push go. `ALLOW_DEV_PUSH=1` is gone, as nothing is left to override. Its tests
  (`scripts/pre-push.test.sh`) follow: 33 cases.

### The GPU's first-use test while it waits for searches (2026-11-08)

- **The problem** (abscls-11cl, found by abscls-8tl1.64): the test ends when the CPU workers and the GPU each have 20 s
  of searches (`SpeedMeter.measured`, no timeout). After a short review, or a few searches on the Analysis board, the
  searches end first. The engine settings then said "In use. Testing its speed against a worker…" while nothing
  searched, until more work came.
- **The decision,** among three: the test keeps design 15's 20 s on each side, and the line says what happens
  while the test waits. The other two were ending the test early with what it measured (a change of the 20 s, which the
  engine repository measured) and leaving the line as it was.
- **The change:** the test's meter knows when the test's seconds grow. They grow only while a search runs on a side
  that has less than its 20 s. `SpeedMeter.measured(seconds, onMeasuring)` calls `onMeasuring` at once and at each
  change, until the test ends or the GPU leaves the pool (`packages/engine/src/pool.ts`, through
  `EnginePool.measureGpu`). `GpuControl` keeps it in the status (`{ state: "testing", measuring }`,
  `packages/analysis/src/gpu.svelte.ts`). The line shows "In use. Testing its speed against a worker…" while the test
  measures, and "In use. The speed test continues with the next searches." while it waits. The 20 s, the result's
  storage, and On and Off did not change. Both sites show the line: it is the shared code's.
- **The code review's change:** the first build counted any task in the pool as a search for the test. A task takes a
  free CPU worker first, and the GPU only when no worker is free. The workers' seconds add up across the workers, so
  they pass 20 s early, and the GPU's seconds decide when the test ends. A search on a worker alone, such as one
  position on the board after a short review, then set the line back to "Testing" while the test did not measure. The
  signal moved from the pool's tasks to the meter's counts.
- **The text:** the wording proposed with the decision said "goes on". The STE skill (strict mode) counts it as a
  phrasal verb (rule 9.3), so the line says "continues". The skill's linter found nothing in either form.
- **Checked,** on the CPU and with fakes only (no GPU run). `packages/engine/src/pool.test.ts`, "the GPU's first-use
  test waits while no search that it needs runs", drives a real pool with a fake clock. A review of 12 s ends, and
  `onMeasuring` gives `false`, `true` and `false`. Ten minutes with no search add nothing. A search on a worker alone
  gives nothing, and the test stays unresolved. The next searches of 8 s end the test while they run, and the ended test
  hears nothing more. `packages/analysis/src/gpu.test.ts` drives `GpuControl` with a fake GPU worker in a real pool. The
  line follows the test through a short review, a worker's search that fails, a worker alone, and the test's end, which
  stores the result once. A GPU search that the engine refuses keeps the GPU, and the line waits again. The line does
  not change after the GPU is lost, after Off, or after the control ends. The idle release in a hidden page brings
  "Waiting: it starts when there is more work than the workers can take."
- **Not covered:** the line in a browser on a GPU. No GPU run was made.

### A click on Cyanotype's board while the view fits again (2026-11-08)

- **The problem** (abscls-0gmp): in whole layout runs beside other jobs, a case of `cyanotype-notes.spec.ts` failed
  twice ("the Analysis board: the notes stay with their position, a pan keeps them, and a click clears them"). A
  right-click on the Analysis board drew an arrow, not a highlighted hex. Alone, the case passed.
- **The cause, in the page:** the note's ends were the hexes under the pointer at the press and at each move, with no
  rule in pixels. The view fits the anchor hexes of the position's legal moves too, and the review asks the engine for
  those rules at each new position (`ReviewView.svelte`). The answer comes from the engine's worker, later on a busy
  machine, and the view then fits again. If it came while the right button was down, the same point of the window
  showed another hex, and the click became an arrow. A player on a slow machine, or with the engine busy, could get
  the same arrow from a click just after a step to another position. So the page was wrong, not the test.
- **The same cause, other clicks:** a left click and a tap take their hex at the release, in the view of that moment.
  The review shows a position's candidates from its stored results at once, before the rules. So a click on a
  candidate, pressed before the rules came and released after them, found another hex: it pinned no candidate. The
  board editor gets no rules, so its view does not fit again under a click. A click in a hand takes the hex in the
  hand's own frame, which the rules do not move. The hands' panel can move to another corner when the rules come,
  also under a press on a hand. The click is then lost: it takes no hex, and no other hex.
- **The change:** while a pointer is down on the board, the view keeps its fit, and it fits again after the release
  (design 33, "How the board takes a move", item 1). A move of the hands' panel to another corner waits for the
  release too. So every press reads its hexes in one view, as on chessground's board, which never moves under the
  pointer. Each press that the board takes captures its pointer, so that its release comes to the board. The board
  editor's right press did not capture it before. A lost capture ends the press as a cancel does. A press on a hand
  does not keep the panel in its corner. To keep it there, the panel must wait for the hand's click, which comes
  after the release.
- **First tried:** a right press that moved less than the board's `DRAG_PX` (4 pixels) was a click, whatever the hex
  under the pointer. It fixed the right-click alone, and chessground's shapes have no such rule. The view that keeps
  its fit under a press replaced it.
- **Measured,** on the CPU in headless Chromium. CDP's CPU throttling (6 times) did not reproduce it: 10 of 10 passed,
  since it slows the page and not the engine's worker. A test held the workers' messages and stepped to the next
  position. It pressed the right button, then gave the rules. The view then fitted again: the board's `viewBox` grew
  from 42 to 49 units wide. Before any change, the test failed 5 of 5, each with an arrow. With the 4-pixel rule it
  passed 5 of 5. Two cases of `cyanotype-notes.spec.ts` now delay the workers' messages. One right-clicks on the
  Analysis board, and checks that the view keeps its fit under the press and fits after the release. The other
  clicks a candidate's rank on the review, and checks that the click pins the candidate that it pressed. Each case
  waits until the reply with the rules is among the delayed messages, and then presses. Against the build with the
  4-pixel rule, both failed 2 of 2. The view grew from 42 to 49 units wide under the right press, and the click
  pinned nothing. With the view's hold, `cyanotype-notes.spec.ts` passed 18 of 18 (`--repeat-each=3`).

    60, turn 31, Blue's edit `1:0,0>2:-3,5`). It also reaches 3 turns in the other order (turns 25, 26 and 33, each

    were the engine's first choice, with the second choice at least 0.10 worse (`ONLY_MOVE_GAP`). The screen found 3
    such moves in the game's first 43 moves, and none in the test game's first 38. Its review at Lite reaches a Great
    by move: move 39, turn 20, Red's capture `2@-27,-17`. The screen stopped after this game, and did not search seeds
    13 and 14. `selfplay.mjs --seed 12` plays the same game again: the record that it wrote again was the committed
    one, byte for byte.
- **The stored reviews:** `apps/hedgeschool/scripts/cyanotype-review-fixture.mjs` writes them after
  `cyanotype-review.json`, at the same visits, in headless Chromium with the layout test's launch options and the

  the first turns' results from the store, so the two files give those positions the same results. A review of
  another game runs in a new browser context. Each file keeps the results of its own review, as a review file keeps
  them (`@abstractclass/analysis/files.ts`, `belongs`): each position of the record, and the positions one move from
  them, which the review searches to confirm a Great. With the files as arguments, the script writes only those, from

  (241 results: `tests/fixtures/cyanotype-whole-review.json`). The game of seed 12 took 1,358 s (92 results:
  `tests/fixtures/cyanotype-seed12-review.json`). The search is `91ab0b7d`, and the network is Stamp Duty 0.2.
- **No ownership in these files:** each result's ownership (4,492 numbers, for the area map) was two thirds of their

  So the script writes them without it, and `cyanotype-review.json`, which the browser tests load, keeps it. The whole

  0.42 MB (0.15 MB to 0.05 MB). Hedge School's largest stored review, `hedgefund-review.json`, has 1.4 MB (0.30 MB

### Cyanotype's cells: striped walls and six-point stars (2026-11-08)

Cyanotype's star cells had a white five-point star, and its walls white courses of bricks. A lab (abscls-8tl1.67)
showed five designs of the marks on the same position: the board fixture "A capture" of Stamp Duty's game. It showed
each design on the Analysis page at 1,280 pixels in both themes, on the board at 360 pixels, in the hands, and in a
move list's row with a star cell's edit.

- **The earlier marks:** a five-point star, and a wall's bricks. Their thin lines blur in a move's glyph, which
  draws a cell about 15 pixels high, and on a faded cell.
- **strategyjam.org's cells,** redrawn: pale Normal cells joined into one shape, a hatched star cell, and a smaller
  solid wall with a plate and six rivets. They redraw another site's artwork closely, so a public site needs its
  makers' consent to ship them.
- **Six points and a rampart:** a six-point star that shares the hex's six corners, and a wall with a thick dark
  rim. The star fills more of the cell and reads at text size. In the dark theme, the rim blends into the dark board.
- **A jewel and stripes:** a round white disc, and three diagonal white stripes. They are the two simplest marks
  that stay apart at text size and in grey: a shape against lines.
- **A hollow star cell and a notched wall:** each kind changes the cell's body. At small sizes the notched wall
  looks like a gear.

The choice is the jewel and stripes, with the six-point star in place of the jewel:

- **Both marks read at text size and in grey.** A move's glyph, a captured cell and a ghost show them as clearly
  as the board does.
- **The six-point star is round and shares the hex's corners.** It has the hex's symmetry, so it sits in the middle
  of the cell with no offset. It fills more of the cell than the jewel, and it keeps the shape that the kind's name
  gives.
- **Stripes against a star: lines against a shape.** The two marks differ in their kind, so they stay apart for a
  reader who does not see the colours. The rampart is not taken: the stripes need no rim, and the rim blends into
  the dark theme's board.

Cell.svelte draws this one design. The lab's choice of a design (the address's `?cells=`, and a bar on each page)
does not ship. No layout case changes: no case takes a picture of the cells or selects a mark. The logo, the link
preview picture and the strategyjam.org button keep their own five-point star, and the picture keeps its walls'
bricks. Design 33, "The cells' marks", has the marks' sizes.

### Cyanotype's move list by turn: a turn's judgement cell on its last move's row (2026-11-08)

Design 33 ("The review and the Analysis board", item 3) changed (abscls-8tl1.66). Cyanotype's move list has one move
a line. By turn, the turn's judgement cell (its quality label, the ◆ and the loss) stood on the row of the turn's
first move. The judgement cell is a button that acts as the turn's last move. So after a turn of two moves, the move
on the board showed on two rows: the second move on its own row, and the judgement cell on the first row.

- **The change,** in the shared view (`packages/review/src/ReviewView.svelte`): with one move a line, the judgement
  cell stands on the row of the turn's last move. A turn of two moves has it on its second row. A turn of one move
  (Blue's first turn, or a turn that ends the game) has it on its one row. The cell now has its column and no row.
  It comes after the turn's moves, so the grid puts it on the last move's row. The move on the board and its
  judgement cell now light on one row. Hover, the turn's group light, the place kept in view and the move menu are
  as before.
- **Where:** the review by turn, and the Analysis board with "Quality labels by" a turn. Both use the shared view.
- **Not changed:** the move lists by move, Practice's move list, and Hedge School. Hedge School has a turn's two
  moves in one row, and its judgement cell in a column of its own.
- **The check:** `cyanotype-review.spec.ts`, in the review by turn at 1,376 and at 390 pixels. Each turn's judgement
  cell lies within its last move's box from top to bottom, to a pixel. After turn 4, the two lit boxes (the second
  move and the judgement cell) pass the same check. The test does not open the Analysis board.
- **The tops are not equal,** as they were not on the first row before. The cell and the move stand on one
  baseline, and a cell with no label badge is shorter than a move. At 1,376 pixels by turn, the cell is 16.8 pixels
  high, and the move is 21 pixels (Text) or 21.9 (Glyphs). So the cell's top is 3.0 pixels lower in Text and 3.8 in
  Glyphs. Beside an edit in Glyphs it is 6.5 pixels lower, because an edit's baseline is its picture's lower edge.
  A cell with a badge is 0 to 0.8 pixels lower. The cell's own look did not change.

### Cyanotype's review searches the end of an unfinished game (2026-11-09)

Cyanotype's review of an unfinished game took the position after the last move as the game's end (abscls-2pge).
Blueprints' position gave `over` only where the game ends (`apps/cyanotype/src/lib/review/blueprints.ts`). The shared
analysis takes a position with no `over` as the end, in two places. The analysis searches the end only where `over` is
false (`analysis.svelte.ts`, `passCount`), so it did not search that position. The review takes a missing `over` as
the end (`model.ts`, `review`), so it judged the last move and the last turn by the scores there, as a result.
Blueprints' own ending text takes a missing `over` as no end (`endingText`, `over ?? false`), so the page called the
game unfinished while its labels took the game as ended. Hedge School's position always gives `over`, so its review of
an unfinished game searched the end.

- **The fix:** Blueprints' position gives `over: !!outcome`, as Hedge School's gives `over: outcome !== null`.
  `endingText`'s own rule (`over ?? false`) reads the same with it.
- **`over` is required:** in the game interface's `PositionInfo` (`@abstractclass/analysis/game.ts`, design 29), and
  in each site's position type (Blueprints' `Position`, Enclosure's in `enclosure.ts`). So a site's code cannot build
  a position without it. Two places in Hedge School built a position without it: a lesson's board before the engine
  draws it (`lessons.ts`, `lineBoard`) and the image caption's test. Both now give `over: false`, as they read before.
  Both sites build and type-check. The type check does not see one input: Hedge School's sample game
  (`mock/review.json`) has no `over`, and `mock/sample.ts` casts it to the review's data. The review reads its end as
  the game's end by its default (`over ?? true`), which is right for that finished game.
- **The test:** `blueprints.engine.test.ts` reviews the test game to move 39 from the engine's positions. Each position
  says `over: false`, and the review takes the end's win chance from its search. On the code before the fix, the
  position said nothing.
- **The stored reviews:** `cyanotype-review-fixture.mjs` wrote them again, through `scripts/machine run` with 2
  threads, on the CPU. The review to turn 20 took 973 s, the whole game 1,830 s, and seed 12's game to turn 23
  1,138 s. Each review of an unfinished game gained 2 results, the end at 32 and at 512 visits: 79 to 81 in
  `cyanotype-review.json`, and 92 to 94 in `cyanotype-seed12-review.json`. Every other result is the same, byte for
  byte. The whole game's file did not change, except its date, so it stays as it was.
- **The labels:** the end of the review to turn 20 has its search, Red's win chance 0.704 at 512 visits. The whole
  game's review has the same result there. Turn 20 starts at Red's 0.811, so the turn loses 0.107: it is a Mistake,
  not Excellent. Before, the review read Red's 1.000 at the end, a gain. Move 39 goes from Red's 0.691 to 0.704: it
  stays Excellent. In `cyanotype.txt`, only turn 20 moved (labels by turn: Excellent 5 to 4, Mistake 6 to 7). Now it
  has the labels of `cyanotype-whole.txt` for moves 1 to 39 and for turns 1 to 20. No label of the game of seed 12
  moved: its last turn (turn 23) and its last move (move 45) stay Mistakes.
- **The browser tests:** `storedResults` (`cyanotype-review.ts`) takes the position after the last move too, as the
  live review of turns 1 to 3 now searches it. The label snapshot's test checks a stored result for each position that
  the review searches (`passCount`).

### The candidates table's column widths, measured on Cyanotype (2026-11-08)

How well do the widths of the candidates table's columns fit their content? The table (`engineTable` in
`packages/review/src/ReviewView.svelte`) is fixed: its colgroup gives Rank (#) 1.75rem, Win chance (its header "Blue
wins" or "Red wins") 4.5rem, Lead 4.75rem and Visits 3rem, and the Move column takes the rest. Each cell is cut at
its end. Both sites share the colgroup. The measurement is `apps/hedgeschool/scripts/measure/table-widths.mjs`
(abscls-8tl1.68).

- **What ran:** headless Chromium on Windows, with `playwright.config.ts`'s launch options (off the GPU), on a
  Cyanotype build of dev at 7760ccb (engine-91ab0b7d, `VITE_EDITION=early`). The page held the stored review of the
  test game (Stamp Duty against itself, to turn 20) and searched nothing. The script read the table at each of the 39
  positions, by move, at 360, 390, 768, 1,024, 1,280, 1,376 and 1,920 pixels, in each Move notation (Glyphs and
  Text): 666 rows a width. Where the window has an Analysis tab (below 1,260 pixels), the script opened it.
- **What did not run:** Hedge School's table, since this measurement had no preview of Hedge School. Fonts other
  than Windows' Segoe UI. The table's font is `system-ui`, so macOS, iOS and Android draw it in other fonts, whose
  widths this measurement did not see.
- **The widest possible values,** measured in the first row's semibold: a lead from 1,000 on is written short ("Blue
  +1.2k"), so a lead never has more than three digits before its letter. The position on screen takes up to 16,384
  visits, so Visits can have five digits. Win chance runs to "100.0%".

The fixed columns, the same at every width and in both notations, in pixels. "Room" is the cell less its padding of
4 pixels a side. "Fits all" is the widest of the header, the values seen and the values possible, with the padding.

| Column | Column | Room | Header | Widest value seen | Cut | Left over: median / least | Widest possible | Fits all |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---:|---|---|---:|
| Rank (#) | 28 | 20 | 8.3 (#) | 17.4 (10) | 0 of 666 | 5.5 / 2.6 | – | 25.4 |
| Win chance | 72 | 64 | 60 (Blue wins) | 39.1 (49.4%) | 0 of 666 | 26.9 / 24.9 | 44.1 (100.0%) | 68 |
| Lead | 76 | 68 | 30 (Lead) | 62.7 (Blue +104) | 0 of 666 | 16 / 5.3 | 65.4 (Blue +1.2k) | 73.4 |
| Visits | 48 | 40 | 33.4 (Visits) | 23.7 (394) | 0 of 666 | 32.5 / 16.3 | 37.1 (16384) | 45.1 |

The Move column, in pixels. "Smaller" is a name drawn below its full size and not cut, down to the least size of 65%.

| Notation | Width | Move | Room | Full size | Smaller | Least size | Median smaller size | Cut | Widest at full size |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Glyphs | 360 | 40 | 32 | 0 | 20 | 65% | 65% | 646 | 139.9 |
| Glyphs | 390 | 70 | 62 | 273 | 107 | 65% | 65% | 286 | 139.9 |
| Glyphs | 768 | 448 | 440 | 666 | 0 | 100% | – | 0 | 139.4 |
| Glyphs | 1024 | 153 | 145 | 666 | 0 | 100% | – | 0 | 139.4 |
| Glyphs | 1280 | 101 | 93 | 380 | 286 | 66% | 71% | 0 | 139.8 |
| Glyphs | 1376 | 101 | 93 | 380 | 286 | 66% | 71% | 0 | 139.8 |
| Glyphs | 1920 | 187 | 179 | 666 | 0 | 100% | – | 0 | 139.4 |
| Text | 360 | 40 | 32 | 0 | 20 | 65% | 65% | 646 | 109.2 |
| Text | 390 | 70 | 62 | 273 | 206 | 65% | 67% | 187 | 109.2 |
| Text | 1280 | 101 | 93 | 480 | 186 | 85% | 92% | 0 | 109.2 |
| Text | 1376 | 101 | 93 | 480 | 186 | 85% | 92% | 0 | 109.2 |

At 768, 1,024 and 1,920 pixels every name in Text is at full size too.

- **Rank (#): about right.** The widest rank seen, "10" in its badge, leaves 2.6 pixels. The table's rank has no
  "+N": that chip is on the hands (glossary, "Rank chip"). A narrower column would leave less than a pixel.
- **Win chance: too wide for its values.** No value is cut, but the values leave 24.9 pixels at least: the header
  "Blue wins" (60 pixels) sets the width, not the values (44.1 pixels at most).
- **Lead: about right.** No lead is cut. The widest lead seen, "Blue +104", leaves 5.3 pixels, and the widest
  possible, "Blue +1.2k", leaves 2.6. A lead of four digits never shows, since the table writes it short.
- **Visits: about right, with a little room.** No value is cut. The stored review has at most 394 visits a
  candidate, but the column must hold five digits, which leave 2.9 pixels.
- **Move: too narrow on phones and in a wide window's side column.** At 360 pixels 646 names of 666 are cut, and at
  390 pixels 286 in Glyphs. At 1,280 and 1,376 pixels 286 names in Glyphs are smaller than full size, down to 66%.
- **The margins are thin for other fonts.** Rank, Lead and Visits fit their widest value by 2.6 to 2.9 pixels in
  Segoe UI. A font about 4% wider would cut "Blue +1.2k". No other font was measured.

**The proposal (not decided):** only the Win chance column changes. It becomes 3.5rem (56 pixels), and its header
becomes "Win %" (41 pixels), so that "100.0%" fits with 3.9 pixels left. The other columns keep their widths, since
each fits its widest possible value with less than 3 pixels to spare. "Blue %" (43.3 pixels) also fits, and keeps the
mover's name in the header. A title on the header, "Blue's win chance", would say whose chance it is. The script's
`--lab` draws the proposal into the page, as a style sheet and the header's text, not in the site's code. With it:

| Notation | Width | Move | Room | Full size | Smaller | Least size | Median smaller size | Cut |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Glyphs | 360 | 56 | 48 | 20 | 351 | 65% | 68% | 295 |
| Glyphs | 390 | 86 | 78 | 373 | 7 | 65% | 65% | 286 |
| Glyphs | 1376 | 117 | 109 | 380 | 286 | 78% | 83% | 0 |
| Text | 360 | 56 | 48 | 20 | 351 | 65% | 71% | 295 |
| Text | 390 | 86 | 78 | 380 | 280 | 71% | 77% | 6 |

The Move column gains 16 pixels at every width. At 360 pixels the names cut fall from 646 to 295, and at 390 pixels
in Text from 187 to 6. At 1,376 pixels the smaller names in Glyphs go from 66% to 78% at least, and in Text the
smaller names fall from 186 to 48. In Glyphs at 390 pixels the edits stay cut: an edit at 65% needs about 91
pixels. 1,280 pixels reads as 1,376 does. No Lead, Win chance or Visits value is cut.

**On Hedge School,** the table shares the colgroup and the header, so its Edge column gains the same 16 pixels and
its header reads "Win %" too. Its leads are in points and much shorter than Blueprints', so the Lead column fits them.
Its names are 5 to 7 characters in a slot of 4.1em, drawn down to 70% of their size. Not measured: by arithmetic, at
360 pixels the cell's room grows from 32 to 48 pixels, which holds a name at 75% of its size (43.4 pixels), where now
it is cut.

### The Lead column in a wide window, measured on Cyanotype (2026-11-08)

The Win chance column keeps its 4.5rem and its header "Blue wins": the proposal of the entry above is not taken. The
question now: in a wide window the Lead column looks too narrow, while the Move column has room to spare. Where does
Move have room, and how wide should Lead be there? The measurement is the same script,
`apps/hedgeschool/scripts/measure/table-widths.mjs`, which now takes a window as `WxH` (abscls-8tl1.68).

- **What ran:** headless Chromium on Windows, with `playwright.config.ts`'s launch options (off the GPU), on a
  Cyanotype build of dev at 5cd6b41 (`VITE_EDITION=early`), with the stored review of the test game. The script read
  the table at each of the 39 positions in Glyphs and in Text, in 16 windows: 390, 768, 1024x768, 1152x864, 1259x800,
  1260x800, 1280x800, 1366x768, 1376x768, 1376x952, 1440x900, 1536x864, 1600x900, 1680x1050, 1920x960 and
  1920x1080. Then it read them again with the proposal, from a style sheet of the script's `--lab`, at those windows
  and 360.
- **What did not run:** Hedge School's table. Fonts other than Windows' Segoe UI. The script measured the widest
  possible lead in Arial too, as a stand-in for a wider font. Arial has no semibold, so the first row's semibold
  comes out as Arial's bold, which is wider than a true semibold: the stand-in errs to the wide side.

**The Lead values.** No lead is cut in Segoe UI, at any window. The widest lead seen is "Blue +104" (62.7 pixels, after
move 10), in a room of 68 pixels: 5.3 pixels are left. Leads of 100 or more are common in the game's second half: all
five rows in view after move 36 have them. The widest possible lead is "Blue +1.2k" (65.4 pixels, and 69.7 in the Arial
stand-in, which is cut). A lead from 1,000 on is written short, so a lead never has four digits. The cell shows no
"±" part. So Lead is not too narrow for its values in Segoe UI, but it is tight: the gap from a lead's end to the
Visits column's text is 13.3 pixels at least, where Win chance's gap is 32.9. A wider system font can cut it.

**Where the Move column has room.** The panel has three layouts (`ReviewView.svelte`): one column below 800 pixels,
two columns (board and side) from 800, and three (summary, board and side) from 1,260. In two and three columns the
side column is 364 to 460 pixels wide. On Cyanotype the board is a square as high as the window allows, so the
window's height sets the side column's width as much as its width does. The table is the side column less 49
pixels. Move is what the table leaves after 224 pixels of the other columns. The widest name at full size is 139.9
pixels in Glyphs and 109.2 in Text. Measured, in pixels. "Spare" is the least room that the names leave at full size, a
negative number where names are drawn smaller.

| Window | Side | Table | Move | Spare, Glyphs | Spare, Text |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 390 | 343 | 294 | 70 | −77.9 | −47.2 |
| 768 | 721 | 672 | 448 | 300.6 | 330.8 |
| 1024x768 | 426 | 377 | 153 | 5.6 | 35.8 |
| 1152x864, 1259x800 | 460 | 411 | 187 | 39.6 | 69.8 |
| 1260x800, 1280x800, 1376x952 | 374 | 325 | 101 | −46.8 | −16.2 |
| 1366x768 | 431 | 382 | 158 | 10.6 | 40.8 |
| 1376x768 | 436 | 387 | 163 | 15.6 | 45.8 |
| 1440x900 | 411.5 | 362.5 | 138.5 | −8.4 | 21.8 |
| 1536x864 to 1920x1080 (5 windows) | 460 | 411 | 187 | 39.6 | 69.8 |

So Move has room to spare where the side column is wide: in one column from about 480 pixels, and in two or three
columns where the window is wide for its height (such as 1,152 by 864, 1,376 by 768, and 1,536 by 864 or wider). At
1,024 by 768 and 1,366 by 768 the names leave only 5.6 and 10.6 pixels in Glyphs. A window as tall as 1,376 by
952 leaves the side column at its least, and its names in Glyphs are already drawn down to 66%: there Move has no
room to give. One window width can fall on either side (1,376 by 768 has room, 1,376 by 952 has none).

**The proposal (not decided):** the Lead column becomes 5.5rem (88 pixels) where the table is at least 24rem (384
pixels) wide, and keeps 4.75rem where it is narrower. The rule goes by the table's width, not the window's, since the
height decides the side column's width too. In the site's code it is a container query: `@container` on the table's
box and `@min-[24rem]:w-22` on Lead's `col`. 24rem is the four other columns (28, 72, 88 and 48 pixels) and the
test game's widest name in Glyphs at full size with its cell's padding (148 pixels): above it, every name of the test
game keeps its full size. A longer name can still be drawn smaller there: the longest edit of the strategyjam.org
archive is 142.8 pixels in Text (`apps/cyanotype/src/lib/review/table.ts`), and at 24rem the Move column has 140
pixels of room. 88 pixels give every lead room: "Blue +104" leaves 17.3 pixels, "Blue +1.2k" 14.6, and the Arial
stand-in 10.3. The gap from a lead to Visits is then 25.3 pixels at least, nearer Win chance's 32.9. With the
proposal (`--lab`):

- Lead is 88 pixels at 768, 1152x864, 1259x800, 1376x768 and from 1536x864 to 1920x1080, and 76 at the other windows.
  No value of any column is cut.
- In those windows every name is still at full size, in both notations: in Glyphs the least spare is 27.6 pixels in
  a side column of 460, and 3.6 at 1376x768.
- At every other window measured before and after (390, 1024x768, 1260x800, 1280x800, 1366x768, 1376x952 and
  1440x900) each number of the table is the same as before: the container query changes nothing there. At 360 the
  numbers are those of the entry above.

**On Hedge School,** the table shares the colgroup, so the rule applies there too. Not measured: by arithmetic, its
Edge column gives 12 pixels only where it keeps at least 148, far more than its names of 5 to 7 characters need. Its
leads are in points and short, so they gain only room.

The crops (the script's `--crops`, not committed) show the position after move 36, in Glyphs, light and dark: all
five rows in view have three-digit leads ("Red +140" to "Red +160") and four have two-move names. At 1,376 by 768
and 1,920 by 1,080 Lead widens and every name keeps its size. At 1,376 by 952 the before and after crops are the
same.

**Built.** The proposal is taken as it stands: Lead is 5.5rem where the candidates table is at least 24rem wide, and
4.75rem where it is narrower. Win chance and the other columns keep their widths. In the shared colgroup
(`packages/review/src/ReviewView.svelte`, `engineTable`), the table's box is a named container
(`@container/candidates`), and Lead's `col` has `w-19 @min-[24rem]/candidates:w-22`. The name keeps the query on
the box, also if a container is added later between the box and the `col`. The box keeps room for its scroll bar
at all times, and a container query reads the box's content width, which leaves that room out. So the query reads
the table's own width. Measured in the built site (headless Chromium, `playwright.config.ts`'s launch options, off
the GPU), the box's content width and the table's width are the same at every window, on both sites. The query
takes the box as meant: at 1,024 by 768 (a table of 377 pixels) and 1,366 by 768 (382) Lead stays 76 pixels, and at
1,376 by 768 (387) it is 88. A query on the box with its scroll bar's room (392 and 397 pixels) would widen Lead at
the first two.

**Cyanotype, measured in the built site.** The script ran on a Cyanotype build of the change on dev at a2f5be8
(`VITE_EDITION=early`), at the windows of the measurement above and 360, in Glyphs and Text. Each number is the same as
in the `--lab` run. Lead is 88 pixels at 768, 1152x864, 1259x800, 1376x768 and from 1536x864 to 1920x1080, and 76 at
360, 390, 1024x768, 1260x800, 1280x800, 1366x768, 1376x952 and 1440x900. No value of any column is cut. Where Lead
widens, every name keeps its full size: in Glyphs the least room left is 27.6 pixels in a side column of 460 and 3.6
at 1376x768. "Blue +104" leaves 17.3 pixels. A phone keeps the widths of before: at 360 and 390 each number is the
same as in a build of dev.

**Hedge School, measured.** The script now also opens Hedge School's review (`--site hedgeschool`): the review file of
the layout test (`tests/fixtures/hedgefund-review.json`, 120 edges), read at every position in the default edge
notation, at the same windows, on a build of dev and on a build of the change. Hedge School's side column is as wide as
Cyanotype's at most windows (447 pixels at 1680x1050, 458 at 1152x864, 402 at 1440x900). Lead widens at the same
windows as on Cyanotype. Its leads are in points, and in the second half of this game they have three digits (the
widest, "Blue +114", 62.7 pixels). No Lead value is cut: they leave 5.3 pixels at least at 76 pixels, and 17.3 at 88.
The Edge column's names are 5 to 7 characters (62.7 pixels at most), and they keep their full size at every window
from 768 on, before and after. The least room that they leave, in pixels:

| Window | Lead | Edge column, dev | Edge column, with the change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|

Two cuts on Hedge School do not come from the column widths, and are the same on dev: the rank of a 100th candidate

**The named container, measured again.** The numbers above are from a build in which the box is a container with no

The crops (the script's `--crops`, not committed) show the table at 1,376 by 768 and 1,920 by 1,080, light and

### Cyanotype's board editor checks that a game can reach the position (2026-11-09)

Design 33 ("Decision", item 10, "The engine's files", items 1 and 2, "The board editor", item 6, and "The gaps from
Hedge School"), design 29 and design 21 changed (abscls-8tl1.59). Cyanotype takes Blueprints' release
`engine-887be290` (request 28, the engine repository's abscls-0dh7, its `games/blueprints/docs/decisions/port.md`,
entry of 2026-11-09). Its board editor, its Import and its starts from a link or a file now check that a game can reach
a set-up position, as Hedge School's do (its design 21, item 10, with Enclosure's protocol 0.5).

- **The lock** (`apps/cyanotype/engine.lock.json`): the four files that the release changed come from `engine-887be290`:
  the module and the GPU module (build `887be290`, protocol 0.8.0, search `91ab0b7d`) and the two practice bots
  (interface 0.1.3). The other nine files have the same SHA-256 in the manifests of `engine-91ab0b7d` and
  `engine-887be290` (the two libraries, the evaluator and its two libraries, the notices, the terms, the network and its
  graph), so their entries and their paths stay, and a browser's cache keeps them. No script writes the lock: this
  change edited its entries by hand, as each earlier move did. Each of the 13 entries has its SHA-256 and its size in
  the manifest of `engine-887be290`, and the lock's `sizes` are the manifest's `engine.sizes`. The release's
  `settings.cfg` stays out, as before. `npm run engine -- --deploy` fetched the 13 files with the lock's SHA-256,
  checked the sizes and `maxThreads` against the manifest of `engine-91ab0b7d` (the evaluator's release), and the module
  answered protocol 0.8.0 and the search `91ab0b7d`. Both bots give `minPlayoutsPerThread` 8.
- **Protocol 0.8.0** breaks a 0.7 client: the engine refuses an analysis of a position that no game reaches, with the
  error's field `position` and the reasons. `ROOT_VIEWS_PROTOCOL` is 0.8.0, so the engine package refuses a 0.7 module
  for Cyanotype, as the lock's move needs. `describe` gives `check` for its `position`. describe_game gives none, so the
  site asks describe.
- **The stored results stay:** their keys name the search and the network's SHA-256 (`packages/analysis/src/cache.ts`,
  `analysisKey`), not the release. The pool takes the search that the module reports, and the review's first reads
  take the manifest's `search`, which the lock gives. Both are `91ab0b7d`, as at `engine-91ab0b7d`. A browser test opens
  the stored review of the test game, made with `engine-91ab0b7d`, on the new release with the engine on, and checks
  that the page asks for no search (`tests/cyanotype-review.spec.ts`).
- **The board's lab data** (`src/lib/board/fixtures.json`) made again: only its header changed. Every position, legal
  move and footprint is the same.
- **The shared parts** (design 29, item 11): the position check's type (`PositionCheck`) and its words for a notice
  (`checkProblem`) are in `packages/engine/src/protocol.ts`, and the editor's status
  (`packages/review/src/PositionCheckStatus.svelte`) in the review package. Hedge School's editor and its Analysis
  board use them. Its editor keeps the same words and the same markup as before. Each game's reason keeps its own
  places: Enclosure's `edges` (Hedge School's `EdgeReason`), Blueprints' `hexes` (Cyanotype's `HexReason`).
- **The notices' words** (the review): the notice read "The Analysis board cannot open this position: This position
  cannot occur in a game: …", which says the same thing twice, puts a capital after a colon and joins the reasons
  with semicolons. `checkProblem` now gives the site's lead, then each reason as a sentence of its own, in the
  engine's words. Cyanotype's lead follows the words that say what cannot open: "The Analysis board cannot open this
  position: no game can reach it. Blue's cell on 0,-7 touches Red's cell on 0,-8, …", "cannot load this link: no game
  can reach its start.", and "Cyanotype cannot open these moves: no game can reach their start.". It uses "reach", as
  the editor does. Hedge School's Import shows the problem alone, so its lead is a sentence: "No game can reach this
  position.", then the reasons, with no semicolons. Its Analysis board's notice still puts that sentence after a
  colon ("cannot analyze this position: No game can reach this position."). Hedge School's
  `src/routes/analysis/+page.svelte` builds that notice.
- **A kept board whose start no game reaches** (the review): a board kept in the browser before the check can have
  such a start, and the engine now refuses every analysis of it. Cyanotype's Analysis board checks the kept board's
  start too. When the check fails, a new board opens with the notice "The Analysis board cannot open your own
  analysis: no game can reach its start. … A new board is here instead.", as for a kept board with a komi. A
  browser test keeps such a board and opens the page (`tests/cyanotype-editor.spec.ts`).
- **The editor's marked hexes** (the review): each hex once, as two reasons can name one hex, and the board's
  marks are keyed by hex. A reply of describe without its check is an error ("the engine did not check if a game
  can reach the position"), not a position that passes.
- **Cyanotype's editor** says "A game can reach this position.", or "No game reaches this position:" with each reason
  in the engine's words, and "The hexes each reason names glow on the board." The board draws each named hex with a
  soft fill and ring in the accent colour, over the cells (`Board.svelte`, `targets`), as Hedge School's board makes
  the reasons' edges glow. Analyze needs a position that a game can reach. A finished position that a game reaches
  also says that the game is over.
- **The Analysis board, the Import and the links:** `recordCheck.ts` checks a set-up start with describe before
  anything else (`startChecked`, `startProblem`), and a record's start before its moves (`recordChecked`). So the
  editor's Analyze, a `#position=` address, a link, an analysis file and the Import refuse a start that no game
  reaches, with the engine's reasons, and the board kept here stays. The Import's words for a refused position are
  now "Cyanotype cannot open this position: …", as for moves, since "cannot read" is wrong for a position that the
  engine reads.
- **The reasons' words,** from the engine on the CPU in Node (`recordCheck.engine.test.ts`): one more cell on the
  standard start with no move played gives `start` and its hex. A Red cell beside a Blue cell that is not a wall, in a
  middle game, gives `touch` and both hexes: "Blue's cell on 0,-7 touches Red's cell on 0,-8, and neither is a wall: a
  placement captures each cell of the opponent that touches it, except walls." A Red cell beside two such Blue cells
  gets one reason for both pairs ("2 pairs of Blue's and Red's cells touch, …"), with its three hexes. The same cell
  on the start after 3 moves passes.
- **A game's position goes to the engine as its moves,** and a set-up start keeps its own search: design 33's note
  stays, with request 28's measurement.
- **Left to abscls-8tl1.40:** the practice bot from a set-up start (`blueprints-set-position`, interface 0.1.3), on
  the same lock.
- **Checked:** `npm run check:all` passed every step (the unit tests of both sites and of the packages, with the
  engine's tests on the CPU, none skipped). Hedge School's editor on this branch against dev's preview, in
  Playwright's Chromium, on the standard start and on two positions that no game reaches: the same status text, the
  same markup and the same glowing edges. Each of Cyanotype's 13 engine files, as the local preview serves it, has
  the SHA-256 and the size of the release manifest that its lock entry names. The check of the deployed site
  (`scripts/release-check.mjs`) waits for the deploy. The layout test on the two previews (Chromium): 203 passed,
  1 failed and 5 skipped. The 5 are the analytics cases, which need `VITE_GA_ID`. The failure was the layout case of
  Cyanotype's editor, which waited for the editor's earlier words. Its pattern now takes the new ones, and the case
  passed alone.
- **Checked again after the review:** `npm run check:all` passed all 15 steps, with no test skipped (the engine's tests
  in Node on the CPU). The whole layout test on this branch's two previews (Chromium): 205 passed and 5 skipped, of
  210. The 5 are the analytics cases, which need `VITE_GA_ID`. The 13 cases of `tests/cyanotype-editor.spec.ts`
  passed, the new case of the kept board too.

### Cyanotype's import page keeps the game, as Hedge School's (2026-11-09)

abscls-8tl1.71, from the decision on abscls-8tl1.38's review (2026-11-08): keep the game as Hedge School's import page
does. Design 33, "How a game comes in from strategyjam.org", items 6 and 7, and "The player's games", item 2, give the
result. Design 33's departure "A record after the review's `#`" is gone.

- **Before:** the import page checked the record with the engine's rules (`checkRecord`). "Review the game" then sent
  the record to `/review#record=…`, and the review imported it: the rules checked the same record again, in a second
  worker, before the list kept it. A failure there (blocked site data) showed on the review page.
- **Now:** the import page checks the record once, with each move's capture mark (`checkRecordMarks`). "Review the
  game" keeps the game through the one import (`src/lib/game/import.ts`, `keepChecked`) with that check's answer, so
  the rules do not run again. Then the review opens by the game's id. A failure to keep the game stays on the import
  page, with why. The review checks its game again when it opens, as Hedge School's does: that check is the review's
  own.
- **The failure to keep the game** starts "Cyanotype could not import the game:", and the page says "Importing the
  game…" while it keeps the game: Hedge School's words, since a jam game's site has what Hedge School has. The failure
  shows no line about the tools page. Newer tools do not help a browser that keeps no games. In the same state, Hedge
  School's import page says "You can paste a game record in the Review tab, or bring games from other sites with the
  tools." That line does not help either: the paste uses the same store.
- **The review's `#record=`** gets the Review tab, as on Hedge School (its design 22). Only the import page took the
  game there, and the review took it out of the address at once, so no player holds such a link. The three scripts that
  opened the review there (`scripts/cyanotype-review-fixture.mjs`, `cyanotype-gpu-check.mjs` and
  `cyanotype-gpu-diagnose.mjs` in `apps/hedgeschool`) now paste the game in the Review tab, as the tests do
  (`tests/cyanotype-review.ts`, `pasteRecord`).
- **A link's record** (`/import#record=…`) keeps the choice of a tool's game. Hedge School opens a partner's link in
  the review at once. abscls-8tl1.75 brings the partners' links to Cyanotype.
- **Shared code (design 29, item 11):** the review's opening of a kept game (Hedge School's `Arrival.svelte`, its
  `review(id)`) moved into `@abstractclass/import` as `openReview.ts`. Hedge School's import page and both sites'
  shared reviews use it, with Hedge School's behaviour as before. The rest of Hedge School's arrival step is
  Enclosure's (its analytics, its partners, its sources) or has no part in Cyanotype yet.
- **The Analysis board** still checks the record that its address brings, as for any link to the board: the address
  cannot carry the import page's answer, since a link could claim it.

### The komi's limit on links and files, the Notation row, and a check of the copied caps (2026-11-08)

Design 24, item 15 has the decision. Before, only the record's reader checked the limit (5,052 points either way for
Enclosure, 90,980 for Blueprints).

- **A board's link and an analysis file:** `readBoardLink` (`packages/analysis/src/boardLink.ts`) and
  `readAnalysisFile` (`files.ts`) require the game's limit, and each site passes its record's `MAX_RECORD_KOMI`. One
  helper gives the whole message (`komiLimitProblem` in `packages/record/src/record.ts`). A link gives the record's
  words: "the Komi tag must be from -5,052 to 5,052 points: 6000". A file gives "the analysis file's komi must be
  …", because its komi is a field and not a tag. A site reads the file before `keepAnalyses`, so a refused file puts
  no result in the store. Before, a link at komi 6,000 opened on Hedge School and failed at the engine. Cyanotype
  passes its limit too, before `refuseKomi`, which still refuses any komi there until abscls-8tl1.50.
- **The Notation pages:** each Komi row says that the engine takes a komi from -5,052 to 5,052 points (Cyanotype:
  -90,980 to 90,980), so the site does not read a record beyond that. The numbers come from `MAX_RECORD_KOMI`.
- **One check that a game takes no book:** the review's view asks for the game's opening only where
  `GameAnalysis.takesBook` holds (false on the board and at a komi). `reviewOpening` and the view's `book.opening`
  lose their komi, since the view's check covers both of its calls.
- **The copied caps:** the practice modules pass GTP's `komi` to KataGo's handler, which refuses a komi past
  `Rules::MAX_USER_KOMI` with "unacceptable komi". So the engine step (`checkKomiCap` in
  `packages/engine/src/practice-check.ts`) sends each practice module `komi` at the site's limit either way, and
  half a point past it. It stops when the module refuses the limit, or does not refuse the komi past it with
  "unacceptable komi". The step reads the limit from the site's `src/lib/game/record.ts`. The engine repository
  needs no request for it.
- **Checked:** both engine steps passed with the locked releases: engine-d6786eba's two practice modules at 5,052 and
  engine-91ab0b7d's two at 90,980. Against Hedge School's one-thread module, the check failed at a limit of 5,051 (the
  module took 5,051.5) and at 5,053 (the module refused it), and `komi 6000` gave "? unacceptable komi". A browser
  test (`tests/komi-limit.spec.ts`) opens a link and an analysis file at komi 6,000 on Hedge School's board, and reads
  both Notation rows.

### Cyanotype's analytics and consent, as Hedge School's (2026-11-08)

- **Decided** (abscls-8tl1.48, the owner's decision of 2026-11-06 on design 33's gaps): Cyanotype measures its visits
  and events as Hedge School does, after the visitor's consent, from the shared packages, with Hedge School unchanged
  ([design/33-cyanotype.md](../design/33-cyanotype.md), "Analytics and consent").
- **Moved into the packages:** the analytics (`packages/site/src/analytics.svelte.ts`, a class with each site's
  services and keys), the flag of internal traffic, the ranges, the consent banner, the ask to allow Google Analytics
  in a blocker and their card (with the site's mark as a snippet). The settings' changes went into the analysis
  package, the exports' event into the review's and a practice game's parameters into the practice's. Hedge School's
  files keep their names as wrappers, with its keys, so its pages, events and unit tests stay as they were.
- **The services:** Cyanotype's own Google Analytics property, so that the two sites' reports stay apart: their events
  have the same names. Cloudflare Web Analytics is the domain's one site, `abstractclass.org`, which takes every
  subdomain's beacon and splits the visits by host. The code reads one pair of names in each build (`VITE_GA_ID`,

### The engine step: one engine commit, and each site's komi limit (2026-11-09)

The review of the komi check found three gaps. The step probed the komi cap of the practice modules only. Nothing
held the analysis modules to the same rules. The engine package read the limit from the running site's record, by a
path in the site's folder.

- **One engine commit:** the step stops when the lock's engine modules come from releases of two engine commits or
  more (`checkOneEngineCommit` in `packages/engine/src/lock-check.ts`, design 03). The engine modules are the CPU and
  the GPU module and the practice bot's two modules: the modules that play the rules. The practice evaluator and the
  libraries are not, since they hold no rules. The rule must also pass both locks as they are. Cyanotype takes its
  modules from engine-887be290, and its evaluator, libraries and network from engine-91ab0b7d. Hedge School's
  earlier networks come from wasm-v2-engine-632f2a0. The step logs the commit: d6786eba for Hedge School, 887be290
  for Cyanotype.
- **No practice modules:** the step logs that it checked no komi cap and no `minPlayoutsPerThread`. Both locks have
  practice modules now, so only a unit test gives the line.
- **Each site's limit:** the step is a function, `fetchEngine({ maxKomi })`. Each site's `npm run engine` runs its
  own `scripts/engine.mjs`, which imports its record's `MAX_RECORD_KOMI` and calls the step. An argument of the npm
  script would copy the number into `package.json`, a second source. The site's script keeps the record as the one
  source, and the package imports no site (design 29, item 1).
- **A check of design 29, item 1:** `scripts/package-imports.mjs`, a step of `npm run check:all`, refuses an import
  in `packages/` of a file in `apps/` or of a site's package. It reads literal paths only. The earlier import of the
  record by a computed path was one that it cannot read.
- **Checked:** `npm run check:all` passed, with both engine steps on the locked releases.
- **The review added:**
  - The import check refuses SvelteKit's `$lib` in `packages/` too. A site's build reads that alias as the site's
    own `src/lib`, so a package could import a site's file by it.
  - The import check also refuses a dynamic import of a computed path, the form of the earlier import of the record.
    Four files load the engine's libraries from a site's `static/engine` that way, and one test loads its own module
    again. `COMPUTED_PATHS` in the script names each of these files with what it loads.
  - `fetch-engine.mjs` run alone stops with an error. A site's `package.json` with the earlier command, from a branch
    made before this change, would otherwise do nothing and exit 0. `fetchEngine` also refuses a missing limit.
  - `lock-check.ts` marks every kind of file as an engine module or not, so a new kind does not compile until it is
    marked.
  - The unit tests use the real locks' tags and asset names. One test has Hedge School's lock with engine-c43233eb's
    modules and engine-d6786eba's networks, as abscls-tdbr's branch has it, and that lock passes.
  - Nothing in `packages/` imports a file of `apps/` by any path, a computed one included. `static/engine` is not
    the site's code: the step writes it from the releases.

### The engine step: Practice's CPU form, and each lock as one release's set (2026-11-09)

The step checked each lock's numbers and its engine modules' commit, and started each practice module. Two gaps
stayed. No check ran the threaded bot with its real evaluator, so a bot and an evaluator that do not compute the same
network would pass. And no check held a lock's files to one release's set: the step read only the manifests of the
releases that give a size or a maxThreads, each for its own files. It read no manifest for Hedge School's lock, and
not engine-887be290's for Cyanotype's.

- **Where the check of the CPU form runs:** in the engine step (`checkThreadedBot` in
  `packages/engine/src/practice-check.ts`), not in a browser test. The step runs for both sites, from the package
  (design 29, item 11), at each engine update and before the build, on the exact files of the lock, in Node on the
  CPU. A browser test would need a preview, and the page chooses the bot's form by the browser: on the GPU where it
  has one. Cyanotype's unit test (`apps/cyanotype/src/lib/practice/bot.engine.test.ts`) plays the threaded bot on its
  CPU evaluator at one position of more views, and Hedge School has no such test.
- **What it plays:** the threaded bot with 2 search threads on one evaluator worker, with the manifest's sizes, as
  Practice's CPU form starts it (`botForms.ts`), against the one-thread bot, on the smallest network. The one-thread
  bot runs the network in its own module, so it is the reference. Each start has new bots with the seed 1: a session
  keeps its seed. Both play 6 moves at 1 visit from the standard start, and 6 from a set-up start, the position after
  those moves (`<game>-set-position`, with the rules' one-line position). Each move must be legal by the CPU module's
  `describe`, and the two bots' moves must be the same. Each site's step takes about 5 seconds more.
- **Why 1 visit:** measured on the CPU with both locks, 8 moves a start, new bots for each setting. At 1 visit the
  two bots played the same moves from both starts on both sites. At 4, 8 and 15 visits they parted at some moves with
  the right files, at moves 1 to 6 of a start. A move below 16 visits searches with one thread (design 24, item 14),
  so the difference is not the threads' number. The check compares the network's own moves, which hold.
- **What it catches:** with Enclosure's sizes given to Cyanotype's evaluator, the threaded bot played `2@-9,1` at the
  first move, and the one-thread bot `1:1,1>2:-2,3`. Hedge School's evaluator trapped ("memory access out of bounds")
  with Blueprints' sizes. With a board of 18 it played `A10-D8` at the first move, and the one-thread bot `A10-D9`.
  Hedge School's lock with engine-d6786eba's evaluator and engine-c43233eb's bot passed this check: that evaluator
  computes the same network. The check of the release's set stops that lock.
- **What the moves miss:** a wrong number of policy channels. One too few on Hedge School (47) passed the check's 12
  moves, and the bots parted at move 11 of one longer game. One too many passed 30 moves of one game on both sites
  (49 for Hedge School, 7 for Cyanotype). At 1 visit the bot sends the evaluator one position at a time, and a move
  shows only the policy. The practice bots answer no `kata-raw-nn`: their commands are the start, the position,
  `play`, `genmove`, `undo`, `komi` and the settings, so the check cannot compare the network's raw outputs.
- **The check of a batch's rows** (`checkingRows`): the evaluator evaluates the bot's first batch again with each
  position twice. Each copy must give the position's outputs, within 1e-3. The bot and the evaluator
  place each position of a batch by the evaluator's sizes, so a wrong size moves the second copy. With the right
  files, the copies differed by at most 2e-6 on both sites. With 47 and 49 channels on Hedge School, 7 on Cyanotype
  and a board of 66 on Cyanotype, the policy differed by 15 to 29, and the step stopped. The check costs one
  evaluation of two positions.
- **One release's set** (`checkOneReleaseSet` in `packages/engine/src/lock-check.ts`, design 03): each file of the
  lock must have the SHA-256 and the size that the newest of the lock's releases whose manifest names the file gives.
  The step now reads the manifest of every release of the lock: 5 for Hedge School, 2 for Cyanotype. Both locks pass.
  Every file of Cyanotype's lock has engine-887be290's entry, and every file of Hedge School's lock has
  engine-c43233eb's entry, its earlier networks too.
- **The releases' order:** the time that each manifest was uploaded, from its download's `Last-Modified`. For the
  seven releases of both locks, each was 1 to 10 seconds before GitHub's time of publication (engine-887be290:
  22:03:56 and 22:03:58), and their order was GitHub's. GitHub's API refused this machine (HTTP 403, its 60 requests
  an hour without a token) on the step's first run with it. The cache keeps each time beside its manifest
  (`releases/<tag>/manifest.time`).
- **A limit of the rule:** a new release of an earlier commit, such as a release that changes only the terms, is the
  newest, and its manifest names that commit's modules. A lock that takes its terms from such a release and its
  modules from a later commit would stop the step, though its files are right. Hedge School's engine-d6786eba-terms2
  came before engine-c43233eb, so it does not happen now. The message names both releases. A manifest that is
  uploaded again to an earlier release, to correct it, makes that release the newest too. A machine whose cache keeps
  the earlier time orders the releases as before: the step does not read a cached time again.
- **On CI:** the Tests workflow keeps each lock's download cache by the lock's hash, and a cache that its key finds is
  not saved again. So until a lock changes, the cache has no `manifest.time`, and each run downloads the lock's
  manifests: 5 for Hedge School and 2 for Cyanotype in each job. A failed download stops the step, with the URL and
  the HTTP status or the network's error.
- **Checked:** the unit tests of both checks (fake bots and rules, fake manifests in the real manifests' shape), both
  sites' engine steps on the locked releases, and the mutations above, each put back. The check of a batch's rows:
  `checkThreadedBot` with each wrong size above in the manifest that a script gave it, with no change to a file. A
  failed manifest download (HTTP 504 and 403, no network, no `Last-Modified`), with a fetch that a script replaced:
  each stopped the step with the release, the URL and the cause.

### PostHog in place of Google Analytics (2026-11-09)

- **Decided** (abscls-xb0k): both sites measure with PostHog in place of Google Analytics, in one project for all the
  sites, in cookieless mode always. Cloudflare Web Analytics stays as it is
  ([design/11-early-access.md](../design/11-early-access.md), item 7).
- **Why:** the setup that design 17 needed in Google Analytics (43 custom dimensions, 3 custom metrics, 3 calculated
  metrics, 4 key events and 6 explorations, all by hand) and a consent banner for its cookies were too much, and that
  setup stopped. PostHog's event properties "are used for filtering, breakdowns, cohorts, targeting, and more", with
  no step to register them. Its free plan has 1,000,000 events a month, 1 project and 1 year of data
  (posthog.com/pricing.md, read 2026-11-09). Cloudflare counted about 900 page loads in 350 visits on Hedge School
  from 2026-10-10 to 11-08. With `cookieless_mode: 'always'`, PostHog "never stores PostHog data in cookies or
  local/session storage" and "doesn't require a cookie banner (unless something else on your website uses cookies)"
  (posthog.com/docs/privacy/data-collection.md).
- **The region:** PostHog's US region, the project's region since its signup: the events go to
  `https://us.i.posthog.com`.
  The privacy pages say that PostHog stores the data in the US, and name the basis for the data of visitors from the
  EU, the UK and Switzerland: PostHog's DPA, section 10.3, "Processor confirms that it participates in the EU-US Data
  Privacy Framework, the UK Extension to this Framework and the Swiss-U.S. Data Privacy Framework", with the Standard
  Contractual Clauses of its section 10.4 beside them (posthog.com/dpa and posthog.com/privacy, read 2026-11-09).
- **The client:** posthog-js 1.447.4 from npm, in its slim bundle with no external loading
  (`posthog-js/dist/module.slim.no-external`, with `AnalyticsExtensions` for the page views), not PostHog's snippet. The
  build-sizes check passes either way (no file is near 25 MiB). The snippet loads PostHog's latest `array.js` from
  PostHog's address, and EasyPrivacy, one of uBlock Origin's default lists, blocks it
  (`||i.posthog.com/static/array.js`). The npm client's version is the lockfile's, it loads no script from PostHog, and
  its events' address (`/e/`, with no `ip=`) matches none of the PostHog rules of uBlock Origin's default lists. A site
  imports the client only in a build with the key, so a build without it holds none of PostHog's code.
- **The options** (`packages/site/src/posthog.ts`, each from posthog.com/docs/libraries/js/config.md):
  `api_host: 'https://us.i.posthog.com'`, `defaults: '2026-08-30'`, `cookieless_mode: 'always'`,
  `person_profiles: 'never'` (PostHog's advice for cookieless mode: `identify()` does nothing),
  `capture_pageview: 'history_change'` (the site's pages change without a reload), `disable_capture_url_hashes: true`
  (the review's address names its game's id after the `#`), `autocapture: false`, `disable_session_recording: true`,
  `capture_heatmaps: false` (cookieless mode keeps heatmaps on), `disable_surveys: true`, `capture_dead_clicks: false`,
  `rageclick: false`, `capture_performance: false` (no web vitals: Cloudflare measures the speed),
  `capture_exceptions: false`, `disable_product_tours: true`, `disable_conversations: true`,
  `advanced_disable_flags: true` (no request for feature flags or for the project's remote settings), and
  `internal_or_test_user_hostname: null` (the defaults mark a visit to `localhost` or `127.0.0.1` as a test user,
  which sets a person property: the site makes no persons, and only the live site has the key).
- **What PostHog receives** with each event, as a page view on this branch's build showed it: the address without
  its `#` part, the path, the host, the page's title, the referrer, the browser, its version and language, the
  operating system, the device's type, the time zone, the screen's and the window's sizes, and `$cookieless_mode`
  with the distinct ID `$posthog_cookieless`. The privacy pages name these. No page's title names a game or a player.
- **The events:** design 17's and design 33's, with the same names and parameters, as event properties. The visitor's
  `games_stored` is a super property of the page (`register`): every later event of the page carries it. Cookieless
  mode keeps no person, so it is no person property.
- **The owner's visits:** `?internal=on` stays. A browser with the flag gives every event `internal: true`, the first
  page view too (`register` in `loaded`, which runs before it). The project's filter of internal and test users is
  the owner's step.
- **The consent:** the analytics purpose goes from both sites. Hedge School keeps the games' purpose (design 25: the
  random ID that links a browser's practice games), under its key `hedge-school:consent:2`, and its banner names that
  purpose only, with no "Choose each". Cyanotype asks for no consent: no banner, and no "Your
  choices" on its Privacy page.
- **The ask to allow the measuring in a blocker** (design 27) goes. No visitor accepts PostHog's counts, so a request
  would go to every visitor with a blocker. uBlock Origin's default lists (EasyList, EasyPrivacy, uBlock filters,
  uBlock filters - Privacy, Peter Lowe's list, read 2026-11-09) do not stop the npm client's events. AdGuard's
  tracking protection list (`||i.posthog.com^`) and Firefox's strict tracking protection (Disconnect's Analytics) do.
  posthog-js calls `on_request_error` only for a status of 400 or more, so the page cannot see a blocked request
  without a check of blockers, which design 27 rejects. This departs from the issue's text, which kept the ask if a
  blocker stops PostHog as it stopped Google's tag. The removal is confirmed. The ask can come back with a check of
  its own.
- **The tests:** the layout test's analytics cases (`tests/analytics.spec.ts`, which replaces
  `tests/analytics-ask.spec.ts`) run on check:all's builds: Hedge School's with a made-up key, Cyanotype's without
  one. The tests' Chromium resolves none of PostHog's addresses (`--host-resolver-rules`), and Playwright's routes
  answer them in PostHog's place. posthog-js sends nothing from a browser that looks like a bot: a name or a brand
  with "HeadlessChrome", or `navigator.webdriver`. The analytics cases give their pages a desktop Chrome's name, no
  brands and no webdriver flag. The first run without them received no page view.
- **Not in this change:** the six reports of design 17 as PostHog insights (a later issue, by PostHog's API), and
  Hedge School's release.
- **Checked** (on dev at a96f9776): `npm run check:all` passed, all 16 steps. The layout test (headless Chromium, on
  this branch's previews of both sites) passed all 220 cases, with none skipped: the 4 analytics cases among them.
  Cyanotype's build, with no key, has no file that names PostHog. In Hedge School's build with the made-up key,
  PostHog's client is one chunk of 201,604 bytes (64,697 gzipped), which loads after the page starts.

### Cyanotype's events, tested with PostHog (2026-11-09)

abscls-xb0k, after "Cyanotype counts its review files and review snapshot" (abscls-8tl1.34), whose test read Google's
tag queue, and "PostHog in place of Google Analytics".

### Hedge School's GPU-path check (2026-11-10)

- **What:** Hedge School had no check of its GPU paths, and the release engine-c43233eb (abscls-tdbr) brought a new
  GPU module that nothing had run in the site (abscls-bp3a). `scripts/hedgeschool-gpu-check.mjs` checks the GPU On,
  then Auto, each in a new browser context: the review, the Analysis board with the GPU beside its one worker, and
  Practice's bot, as Cyanotype's check does. With On it also checks the weak walls (design 30, "The weak walls"): the
  Analysis board from the start, 1 worker and the threat on, Space six times, then the key w. The rings must show, no
  request for the walls (`includeWeakWalls`) may reach a GPU worker, one must reach another worker, and the console
  must show no error. The release's GPU module refuses the field (the engine repository's design 19).
- **One module for both sites:** `scripts/gpu-check.mjs` holds the parts, the waits' limits, the run's limit and the
  watchdog of "Cyanotype's GPU-path checks on this machine's GPU". Each site's script gives its preview, its settings'
  key, its test game, its Review tab's paste, its bot's name, its waits and its own parts (design 29: no copies
  between sites). `tests/records.ts` cuts a record to its first turns for both.
- **Two facts of Hedge School that the check takes:**
  - The early edition's test book holds the test game's first 3 turns (positions 0 to 5), and the review takes their
    values from the book with no search. A review of 3 turns took 1 s and searched nothing, so it would give the GPU
    no backlog. The review of On reviews 5 turns: positions 6 to 9 and the game's end are searched.
  - Hedge School's Analysis board opens a record's link at the start unless the link gives `at`, and Cyanotype's opens
    it at the end. Hedge School's script gives the record's edge count as `at`.
- **The run off the GPU** (`--cpu`, the job `abscls-bp3a-cpu-check2`, 2 threads, the headless shell with the layout
  test's flags, a preview of the branch with engine-c43233eb's files): PASS in 91 s. Every part said "This browser
  cannot use the GPU: it has no GPU for WebGPU.", and no GPU worker started. With On, the review of 5 turns took 24 s,
  the board 28 s (5 candidates at the game's position 10), the weak walls 12 s (14 rings, after A10-D9 N11-Q10
  K10-N11 D10-G12 G12-J13 H7-K10, 1 request for them to a CPU worker and none to the GPU), and Practice 3 s (the bot
  "on the CPU workers.", a turn of 1.1 s). With Auto, the review took 2 s (it waits for the GPU's line only), the
  board 21 s, and Practice 2 s.
- **Cyanotype's check on the shared module** (`--cpu`, the job `abscls-bp3a-cy-cpu-check`): PASS in 291 s, as before
  it: with On, the review 143 s, the board 63 s and Practice 7 s, and with Auto, the review 1 s, the board 67 s and
  Practice 8 s.
- **The review's changes:** the browser contexts that a part opens close at the part's end, so that the weak walls'
  board does not search beside Practice's bot. The weak walls' part waits for the rings or for the note that says why
  none show ("Weak walls: not in this engine"), so that a refusal fails with its reason, not at the wait's limit. The
  part's position is not fixed: Space plays the engine's first choice, and the sixth edge was H7-K10 in one run and
  K10-M11 in the next, with 14 rings in both.
- **The runs after the review** (`--cpu`, the job `abscls-bp3a-rv-cpu`): Hedge School's, through the GPU run's
  wrapper with `--cpu`, PASS in 91 s: with On, the review 26 s, the board 21 s, the weak walls 13 s and Practice 3 s,
  and with Auto, the review 2 s, the board 23 s and Practice 2 s. Cyanotype's PASS in 284 s: with On, the review 136 s,
  the board 65 s and Practice 8 s, and with Auto, the review 1 s, the board 64 s and Practice 8 s.
- **The runs on this machine's GPU** (`scripts/machine run --gpu`, 2 threads, Playwright's full Chromium with WebGPU,
  "nvidia blackwell"):
  - The first run (the job `abscls-bp3a-gpu`, on the review's head) failed at On's review alone. The 5 turns ended on
    the default CPU workers ("Review done: 512 visits a move."), and the GPU's line stayed "Waiting: it starts when
    there is more work than the workers can take." The GPU starts only when more searches wait than the workers take
    (design 15, item 1), and the 5 turns made no such backlog. Every other part passed on the GPU, and Auto's test
    gave "7.1 times a worker's speed."
  - The check now reviews On's turns on 1 worker (the site's option `reviewWorkers`), as the board's part does.
    Cyanotype's check keeps its default workers. The run off the GPU (the job `abscls-bp3a-cpu2`) passed in 109 s.

### A Hedge School review file's game comes in as a pasted record does (2026-11-10)

abscls-1adn. Design 13, item 5, says that a load "keeps the game as it keeps a pasted record". Hedge School's
`keep()` in `src/lib/game/reviewFile.ts` refused a game of other rules or from a set-up start, and then kept the
file's game as it was. So, for a game that came in a review file, the engine's rules never checked its moves, its
record got no cut marks, and a browser that cannot keep games gave the player no message. Cyanotype's `keep()` ran
its full import already ("Cyanotype's review files, as Hedge School's").

- **A correction:** that entry says "Hedge School's import keeps the file's game without the engine's rules, as its
  paste does". The second part is wrong. Hedge School's paste (`importRecord` in `src/lib/game/import.ts`) checks the
  game's moves with the engine's rules (`checkMoves`), and keeps the record with its cut marks (`markCuts`).
- **The change:** Hedge School's `keep()` calls `importRecord`, as Cyanotype's does. So a file's game takes the steps
  of a pasted record. The review refuses a game of other rules or from a set-up start. The engine's rules check the
  moves, and refuse a cut mark on a move that cuts nothing. The record gets its cut marks. A browser that cannot keep
  the game gives the paste's message. A refused file keeps nothing: no game, no variations and no results. The Review
  tab puts the message after "Hedge School could not load this file:", as for any file that does not load. A review
  that a partner site sends (`Arrival.svelte`, design 18) takes the same steps. Its page puts the message after
  "Hedge School could not load the review:".
- **A record that has its marks already:** `markCuts` adds a mark only to a move that has none (`markMoves` in the
  record package). So a file's record keeps the marks that it has, and each move that cuts gets a mark where it has
  none. A game that the browser keeps already stays as it is (`saveGame`), as for a paste. `record.test.ts` checks
  the marks.
- **The check in the tests:** `importRecord` takes the engine's check as an argument (`MoveCheck`, `checkMoves` by
  default), as Cyanotype's does. `hedgeSchoolFiles(check)` gives the review files with a test's check, so the unit
  tests run without the engine. The unit tests (`reviewFile.test.ts`) check each refusal: other rules, a set-up start,
  the engine's check and the store. Each refused file holds a variation and a result, and the store keeps none of
  them. The unit tests also check the cut marks. The browser tests (`tests/review-file.spec.ts`) use the engine's own
  rules. The layout test's game gets its cut marks. A file whose fourth edge repeats the first gets the check's
  message and keeps nothing. A browser with blocked site data gets the store's message.
- **Checked:** check:all passed, all 18 steps. The whole layout test (Chromium, an Early Access build) passed 240 of
  240 cases, with no skip and no flaky case. The four cases of `tests/review-file.spec.ts` are among them. A run of
  an earlier form of the change failed one Cyanotype Practice case once (`cyanotype-practice.spec.ts`, "a kept game
  whose network the site does not ship gives way to the settings card"): its status line did not show within 5 s
  after a reload. This change does not touch Cyanotype. The case passed three times of three alone, and in the final
  run.

### The weak walls' colour: a ramp of three hues (2026-11-10)

- **The problem** (abscls-npaa): in a try of the weak walls on dev, the rings' colours of high chances, such as 70%
  and 85%, looked almost the same, and so did some middle and low chances. The ramp had one hue. It was a straight
  line in OKLab, from #c39a3f at 10% to #6b2a00 at 1 on the light board, and from #8f7748 to #ffc94d on the dark
  board. On it, 70% and 85% are 0.055 apart in OKLab on the light board and 0.047 on the dark board.
- **Five forms,** drawn in the real page at design 30's two positions ("Positions that show them"): the Analysis
  board after Space six times (14 rings, from 24% to 80%) and the review fixture after 40 edges (4 rings, from 19% to
  26%). The script drew each form on the light and the dark board, at 1400 and 390 pixels, with a strip of rings at
  10, 20, ... 100%. The browser was headless Chromium with the layout test's launch options, and the walls came from
  a CPU worker.
  - **A:** the ramp of one hue.
  - **B:** four classes of A's hue, from 10, 30, 50 and 75%, their colours at 0, 1/3, 2/3 and 1 of A's ramp. Each
    class's lower end lies in a gap between the chances of the two positions, and 75% puts 70% and 85% in two
    classes.
